1-1.bio:
St. Basil the Great was born in Caesarea of Cappadocia in the fourth century, to a family of saints. Educated in Athens alongside his friend St. Gregory the Theologian, he set aside a brilliant secular career for the monastic life, and later served as Archbishop of Caesarea. He defended the divinity of Christ against Arianism, gave the Church the Divine Liturgy that bears his name, and organized one of the first great centers of Christian charity for the poor and the sick.

One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, he is honored as a father of monasticism and of Christian philanthropy. The Church commemorates him on January 1, a day beloved in Greek tradition, when the vasilopita is cut in his honor.
1-1.desc: Archbishop of Caesarea, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs.
1-1.name: Basil the Great

1-1.bio:
On the eighth day after His birth the Lord Jesus Christ was circumcised according to the Law of Moses and received the name Jesus, as the angel had announced to the Virgin Mary. The Church keeps this feast of the Lord on January 1, together with the memory of St. Basil the Great.

The feast shows Christ's humility in submitting to the Law He Himself had given, and is understood by the Fathers as a foreshadowing of Holy Baptism, the circumcision made without hands.
1-1.desc: Feast of the Circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ on the eighth day after His Nativity.
1-1.name: Circumcision of the Lord

1-1.bio:
St. Gregory the Elder was Bishop of Nazianzus in Cappadocia in the fourth century and the father of St. Gregory the Theologian. Tradition relates that he was converted to the Christian faith through the prayers of his wife, St. Nonna, and was later made bishop of his native city.

He shepherded Nazianzus for many years and, in his old age, was assisted in the episcopate by his son. He is commemorated on January 1.
1-1.desc: Bishop of Nazianzus, father of St. Gregory the Theologian.
1-1.name: Gregory of Nazianzus the Elder

1-1.bio: The Holy Martyr Theodotos is commemorated on January 1. The synaxaria record that he confessed Christ before the pagan authorities and was beheaded for the faith; the details of his time and place have not been preserved.
1-1.desc: Holy Martyr Theodotos, who ended his contest by the sword.
1-1.name: Theodotos the Martyr

1-1.bio:
St. Peter the Peloponnesian, a New Martyr, came from Tripolitsa in the Peloponnese. Tradition relates that after being pressed to deny his faith, he confessed Christ openly before the Turkish authorities and was put to death in the eighteenth century, in Temesvar according to the synaxaria.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs of the Turkish period and is commemorated on January 1.
1-1.desc: New Martyr Peter of the Peloponnese, martyred for Christ in the eighteenth century.
1-1.name: Peter the Peloponnesian

1-1.bio:
St. Telemachos was a monk from the East who, according to the Church historians, came to Rome at the beginning of the fifth century. Entering the amphitheater during the gladiatorial games, he stepped between the combatants to stop the bloodshed and was killed by the crowd.

Tradition relates that the Emperor Honorius, moved by his death, put an end to the gladiatorial games. He is commemorated on January 1.
1-1.desc: Monk who gave his life to end the gladiatorial games in Rome.
1-1.name: Telemachos the Monk-Martyr

1-10.bio:
St. Gregory of Nyssa was the younger brother of St. Basil the Great, born in Cappadocia in the fourth century to a family rich in saints. As Bishop of Nyssa he defended the Nicene faith against Arianism, endured exile for the truth, and took part in the Second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople in 381.

A theologian of great depth, he wrote profoundly on the Holy Trinity, the creation of man, and the soul's endless ascent toward God. He is commemorated on January 10.
1-10.desc: Bishop of Nyssa, brother of Basil the Great.
1-10.name: Gregory of Nyssa

1-10.bio:
St. Dometian was Bishop of Melitene in Armenia in the sixth century, a kinsman of the Emperor Maurice. He governed his Church with wisdom and was sent on missions to Persia, where he helped many come to the faith.

He reposed in Constantinople and is commemorated on January 10.
1-10.desc: St. Dometian, Bishop of Melitene in Armenia.
1-10.name: Dometian of Melitene

1-10.bio:
St. Markianos was a priest of Constantinople in the fifth century, born of a noble family, who spent his wealth on the poor and on the building of churches, among them the church of St. Anastasia. He was made steward of the Great Church.

Tradition relates that he gave even his own clothing to the needy. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 10.
1-10.desc: St. Markianos, priest and steward of the Great Church of Constantinople.
1-10.name: Markianos the Presbyter

1-10.bio:
St. Theosebia was a sister of St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nyssa, from the family of St. Emmelia and St. Makrina. She served the Church as a deaconess and was praised by St. Gregory the Theologian for her holiness.

She reposed in peace in the fourth century and is commemorated on January 10.
1-10.desc: Blessed Theosebia the Deaconess, sister of St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nyssa.
1-10.name: Theosebia the Deaconess

1-10.bio:
St. Antipas was born in Moldavia in 1816 and became a monk on Mount Athos, where he lived for years in the Romanian skete of the Forerunner. He later traveled to Russia and settled at the Valaam Monastery, where he lived in strict solitude and prayer.

He reposed in 1882 and is commemorated on January 10.
1-10.desc: Venerable Antipas of Calapodesti, Athonite and Valaam ascetic.
1-10.name: Antipas of Valaam

1-10.bio: St. Ammonios is commemorated on January 10 as one of the desert ascetics of Egypt who reposed in peace. Tradition remembers him for the strictness of his fasting and the gentleness of his counsel.
1-10.desc: Venerable Ammonios, an Egyptian desert ascetic.
1-10.name: Ammonios the Venerable

1-11.bio:
St. Theodosius the Cenobiarch was born in Cappadocia in the fifth century and came as a young man to the Holy Land, where he embraced the ascetic life. Near Bethlehem he founded a great monastery of the common life, and he was appointed head of all the cenobitic monks of Palestine, whence his title Cenobiarch.

His monastery cared for the sick, the aged, and the poor, joining prayer to works of mercy, and he stood firm for the Orthodox faith in the disputes of his age. He reposed at a great age and is commemorated on January 11.
1-11.desc: Founder of communal monastic life in Palestine.
1-11.name: Theodosius the Cenobiarch

1-11.bio:
St. Theodosios was born in Trebizond in the fourteenth century and became a monk and later abbot of the Philotheou Monastery on Mount Athos. Tradition relates that he was chosen Metropolitan of his native Trebizond, where he served with wisdom during troubled times.

He is commemorated on January 11.
1-11.desc: St. Theodosios, abbot of Philotheou on Athos and Metropolitan of Trebizond.
1-11.name: Theodosios of Trebizond

1-11.bio:
St. Michael of Klops was a fool-for-Christ of the fifteenth century who, tradition relates, was of princely family but concealed his origin and lived at the Klops Monastery near Novgorod in extreme humility. He was granted the gifts of prophecy and miracles.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 11.
1-11.desc: Venerable Michael the Fool-for-Christ of the Klops Monastery near Novgorod.
1-11.name: Michael of Klops

1-11.bio:
St. Nikephoros was a Cretan who, tradition relates, confessed Christ before the Turkish authorities and was put to death for the faith in the nineteenth century.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs of Crete and is commemorated on January 11.
1-11.name: Nikephoros of Crete

1-11.bio:
Sts. Neollina, Domnina and Parthena were virgins of Edessa who suffered martyrdom for Christ. The synaxaria record their names and their steadfast confession, but the details of their contest have not been preserved.

They are commemorated on January 11.
1-11.desc: Holy Virgin Martyrs Neollina, Domnina and Parthena of Edessa.
1-11.name: Parthena, Domnina and Neollina

1-11.bio:
St. Hyginus was Bishop of Rome in the middle of the second century, a Greek by birth according to tradition. He guided the Roman Church during a time of heresies and persecution and is remembered as a martyr in some accounts.

He is commemorated on January 11.
1-11.desc: St. Hyginus, Bishop of Rome in the second century.
1-11.name: Hyginus of Rome

1-12.bio:
St. Tatiana was a deaconess of the Church of Rome who suffered martyrdom in the third century. Raised in a devout home, she served the Church in prayer and in care for the sick and the poor. Arrested in a time of persecution, she confessed Christ with courage and endured many tortures without denying her Lord.

Her steadfastness moved even some of her tormentors toward the faith, according to tradition. Beloved especially in Russia, where her name is widely given, she is commemorated on January 12.
1-12.name: Tatiana

1-12.bio:
St. Mertios was a soldier from Mauretania in North Africa who confessed Christ during the persecution of Diocletian. Refusing to sacrifice to the idols, he was beaten and thrown into prison, where he died of his wounds.

He is commemorated on January 12.
1-12.name: Mertios the Martyr

1-12.bio: St. Euthasia is commemorated on January 12 as a holy woman martyr. The synaxaria preserve her name and confession, but the details of her life and contest have not survived.
1-12.name: Euthasia the Martyr

1-12.bio:
St. Peter Apselamos was a young man from the region of Eleutheropolis in Palestine. During the persecution of the early fourth century he refused to sacrifice to the idols before the governor at Caesarea and was burned alive.

He is commemorated on January 12.
1-12.desc: Holy Martyr Peter Apselamos of Palestine, burned for Christ.
1-12.name: Peter Apselamos

1-12.bio:
Sts. Tigrios and Eutropios were clergy of Constantinople devoted to St. John Chrysostom. After the exile of the saint in 404 a fire destroyed the Great Church, and they were falsely accused of setting it; Eutropios died under torture and Tigrios was exiled.

They are commemorated on January 12.
1-12.desc: Holy Martyrs Tigrios the Presbyter and Eutropios the Reader of Constantinople.
1-12.name: Tigrios and Eutropios

1-12.bio:
St. Eupraxia was a noblewoman of Constantinople in the fourth century, kinswoman of the Emperor Theodosius. Widowed, she withdrew with her young daughter to the Thebaid in Egypt and entered the monastic life at Tabenna, where she reposed in peace.

Her daughter, St. Eupraxia the Younger, is commemorated on July 25. The elder Eupraxia is commemorated on January 12.
1-12.desc: Venerable Eupraxia the Elder of Tabenna in Egypt.
1-12.name: Eupraxia of Tabenna

1-12.bio:
St. Martinian was a disciple of St. Cyril of White Lake in the fifteenth century and later abbot of the Ferapontov Monastery. Called to the Holy Trinity Lavra by the Grand Prince, he served there as abbot before returning to Ferapontov, where he reposed in 1483.

He is commemorated on January 12.
1-12.desc: Venerable Martinian, abbot of Belozersk, disciple of St. Cyril of White Lake.
1-12.name: Martinian of Belozersk

1-13.bio:
St. Hermylos was a deacon who suffered for Christ under the Emperor Licinius in the early fourth century, in the region of Singidunum, the city known today as Belgrade. Refusing to deny his Lord, he was tortured and finally drowned in the waters of the Danube, together with his friend the jailer Stratonikos, who confessed Christ after witnessing his endurance.

The two friends, deacon and jailer, received the crown of martyrdom together. They are commemorated on January 13.
1-13.name: Hermylos

1-13.bio:
St. Stratonikos was the jailer of St. Hermylos at Singidunum, present-day Belgrade, during the persecution of Licinius. Moved by the sufferings of the deacon, he confessed himself a Christian and was tortured with him; the two were drowned in the Danube.

He is commemorated on January 13.
1-13.desc: Holy Martyr Stratonikos, who suffered with St. Hermylos at Singidunum.
1-13.name: Stratonikos the Martyr

1-13.bio:
St. Maximos was born in Lampsacus in the thirteenth century and became a monk on Mount Athos. He lived as a hermit, repeatedly burning his hut and moving on to avoid attachment, for which he was called Kavsokalyvites, the hut-burner; some took him for a fool until St. Gregory of Sinai recognized his holiness.

He was granted the gift of unceasing prayer and reposed in peace around 1365. He is commemorated on January 13.
1-13.desc: Venerable Maximos the Hut-Burner of Mount Athos.
1-13.name: Maximos Kavsokalyvites

1-13.bio:
St. James of Nisibis was a hermit who was made bishop of that city in the fourth century. He attended the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea and, tradition relates, delivered Nisibis from a Persian siege by his prayers. St. Ephrem the Syrian was his disciple.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 13.
1-13.desc: St. James, Bishop of Nisibis, father of the Council of Nicaea.
1-13.name: James of Nisibis

1-13.bio:
St. Jeremiah I was Patriarch of Constantinople in the first half of the sixteenth century, during the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent. He defended the churches of the city against confiscation, traveled to Jerusalem and Sinai to strengthen the faithful, and reposed in 1546.

He is commemorated on January 13.
1-13.desc: St. Jeremiah I, Patriarch of Constantinople in the sixteenth century.
1-13.name: Jeremiah I of Constantinople

1-13.bio:
St. Eirenarchos was a monk of the Boris and Gleb Monastery near Rostov in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, who lived as a recluse in chains and strict asceticism. Tradition relates that he blessed Prince Pozharsky before the deliverance of Moscow in the Time of Troubles.

He reposed in 1616 and is commemorated on January 13.
1-13.desc: Venerable Eirenarchos the Recluse of Rostov.
1-13.name: Eirenarchos of Rostov

1-13.bio:
St. Hilary was Bishop of Poitiers in Gaul in the fourth century. A convert from paganism, he became the foremost defender of the divinity of Christ in the West, was exiled to Asia Minor by the Arian emperor Constantius, and there wrote his treatise on the Holy Trinity.

He returned to his see and reposed in peace. He is commemorated on January 13.
1-13.desc: St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, defender of the Nicene faith in the West.
1-13.name: Hilary of Poitiers

1-14.bio:
St. Nina, Equal-to-the-Apostles, was a young woman of Cappadocia who in the fourth century brought the Gospel to the land of Georgia. Traveling there alone, she lived in simplicity and prayer, carrying a cross woven of vine branches, and through her preaching and her healings the king and queen came to believe, and the whole nation received holy baptism.

Georgia honors her as its enlightener and mother in the faith, and her vine cross remains the emblem of the Georgian Church. She is commemorated on January 14.
1-14.name: Nina

1-14.bio:
The Holy Fathers of Sinai and Raithu were monks living in the deserts around Mount Sinai and on the Red Sea coast who were slain in raids by nomadic tribes. Tradition relates that thirty-eight were killed at Sinai and thirty-three at Raithu in the fourth century, and that similar slaughters occurred again later.

They are commemorated together on January 14.
1-14.desc: The holy monks massacred at Mount Sinai and at Raithu by barbarian raiders.
1-14.name: Fathers slain at Sinai and Raithu

1-14.bio:
St. Sava was a Serbian prince who fled to Mount Athos as a youth and became a monk. With his father, St. Symeon the Myrrh-streaming, he founded the Hilandar Monastery there, and in 1219 he became the first Archbishop of the autocephalous Serbian Church.

He organized the Church and monastic life of his people and reposed in 1236 in Trnovo. He is the most beloved saint of Serbia and is commemorated on January 14.
1-14.desc: St. Sava, first Archbishop of Serbia and founder of Hilandar.
1-14.name: Sava of Serbia

1-14.bio:
St. Theodoulos was the son of St. Nilus the Ascetic. Living with his father among the monks of Sinai, he was carried off in a barbarian raid and later ransomed; tradition relates that he was afterwards ordained and lived in asceticism with his father.

He is commemorated on January 14.
1-14.desc: Venerable Theodoulos, son of St. Nilus of Sinai.
1-14.name: Theodoulos son of Nilus

1-14.bio:
St. Stephen founded the Monastery of Chenolakkos in Bithynia near Chalcedon in the eighth century, after living as a monk in Palestine. He guided a large brotherhood in the ascetic life and reposed in peace.

He is commemorated on January 14.
1-14.desc: Venerable Stephen, founder of the Chenolakkos Monastery near Chalcedon.
1-14.name: Stephen of Chenolakkos

1-14.bio:
St. Platon was consecrated Bishop of Reval in 1917, the first Estonian bishop of the Orthodox Church. In January 1919 he was arrested by the Bolsheviks in Tartu and shot together with priests and laypeople of the city.

He is commemorated on January 14 together with the New Martyrs of Estonia.
1-14.desc: Hieromartyr Platon, first Bishop of Estonia, and the New Martyrs of Estonia.
1-14.name: Platon of Estonia

1-15.bio:
St. Paul of Thebes is honored as the first Christian hermit. Fleeing the persecution of Decius in the third century, he withdrew into the inner desert of Egypt, where he lived unknown to the world for many decades in fasting, solitude, and unceasing prayer.

Near the end of his long life he was found by St. Anthony the Great, who was sent to him by God and later buried him, and through Anthony his hidden life was made known to the Church. He is commemorated on January 15.
1-15.desc: The first Christian hermit saint in Egypt.
1-15.name: Paul of Thebes

1-15.bio:
St. John the Kalyvites was the son of wealthy parents in Constantinople in the fifth century. Taking with him a Gospel book they had given him, he secretly entered a monastery; years later he returned home and, unrecognized, lived as a beggar in a hut at his parents' gate.

Only at his death did he reveal himself by the Gospel book. He is commemorated on January 15.
1-15.desc: Venerable John the Hut-Dweller, who lived unknown at his parents' gate.
1-15.name: John the Kalyvites

1-15.bio:
St. Pansophios was the son of a proconsul in Alexandria who, after his father's death, gave away his wealth and lived as an ascetic in the desert for many years. In the persecution of Decius he was brought before the governor and died under scourging.

He is commemorated on January 15.
1-15.name: Pansophios the Martyr

1-15.bio:
St. Gerasimos Palladas was born in Crete in the seventeenth century and, after serving as Metropolitan of Kastoria and Adrianople, became Patriarch of Alexandria in 1688. Resigning the throne, he retired to Mount Athos, where he reposed in 1714 at the Vatopedi Monastery.

His relics are kept at Vatopedi. He is commemorated on January 15.
1-15.desc: St. Gerasimos Palladas, Patriarch of Alexandria.
1-15.name: Gerasimos Palladas

1-15.bio:
St. Alexander was a monk of the early fifth century who established communities in Syria and later near Constantinople in which the brethren, divided into choirs, kept up unceasing praise of God by day and night; from this they were called the Akoimetoi, the Sleepless Ones.

He reposed in peace around 430 and is commemorated on January 15.
1-15.desc: Venerable Alexander, founder of the monastery of the Sleepless Ones.
1-15.name: Alexander the Akoimetos

1-15.bio:
Sts. Elpidios, Danax and Helen are recorded in the synaxaria as martyrs who confessed Christ and were put to death for the faith. The details of their contest have not been preserved.

They are commemorated on January 15.
1-15.desc: Holy Martyrs Elpidios, Danax and Helen.
1-15.name: Elpidios, Danax and Helen

1-16.bio:
On this day the Church venerates the precious chains of the holy Apostle Peter. The Acts of the Apostles relates how Peter, imprisoned by Herod and bound in chains, was freed in the night by an angel of the Lord, the chains falling from his hands as he was led out past the sleeping guards.

The faithful preserved these chains with reverence, and many blessings were received by those who venerated them with faith. The feast honors the chief apostle and the power of God who looses every bond. It is kept on January 16.
1-16.desc: Veneration of the chains of St. Peter.
1-16.name: Peter

1-16.bio:
St. Nikolaos was born in Mytilene on Lesbos and worked in Constantinople. Tradition relates that after being falsely accused and pressed to accept Islam, he confessed Christ and was beheaded in 1771.

He is commemorated on January 16.
1-16.desc: New Martyr Nikolaos of Mytilene, martyred in Constantinople.
1-16.name: Nikolaos of Mytilene

1-16.bio:
Sts. Speusippos, Eleusippos and Meleusippos were triplet brothers of Cappadocian origin who, tradition relates, were converted together with their grandmother Neonilla and suffered martyrdom in Gaul in the second century. Several others were converted by their example and martyred with them.

They are commemorated on January 16.
1-16.desc: Holy Martyrs, the triplet brothers of Gaul, and their grandmother Neonilla.
1-16.name: Speusippos, Eleusippos and Meleusippos

1-16.bio:
St. Danax was a reader in the church of a town in Illyricum. When pagans attacked the church he fled with the sacred vessels; captured and ordered to sacrifice to Dionysus, he refused and was beheaded.

He is commemorated on January 16.
1-16.desc: Holy Martyr Danax the Reader, of Illyricum.
1-16.name: Danax the Reader

1-16.bio:
St. Damaskinos was a hieromonk of the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos who was sent to Bulgaria on monastery business. Falsely accused by Turks in Svishtov, he refused to save himself by denying Christ and was hanged in 1771.

He is commemorated on January 16.
1-16.desc: New Hieromartyr Damaskinos of Hilandar, martyred in Bulgaria.
1-16.name: Damaskinos the New

1-16.bio:
St. Romylos was born in Vidin in the fourteenth century and became a disciple of St. Gregory of Sinai at Paroria. He later lived in stillness on Mount Athos and, when the Holy Mountain was troubled by invasions, went to Serbia and settled near the Ravanica Monastery, where he reposed.

He is commemorated on January 16 together with his disciples.
1-16.desc: Venerable Romylos the Athonite, disciple of St. Gregory of Sinai.
1-16.name: Romylos of Ravanica

1-17.bio:
St. Anthony the Great, the father of monasticism, was born in Egypt in the middle of the third century. Hearing in church the Gospel call to sell all, give to the poor, and follow Christ, he gave away his inheritance and withdrew into the desert, where he spent the rest of his long life in prayer, labor, and fierce spiritual struggle.

His holiness drew multitudes, and the desert became a city of monks who took him as their guide. His life, written by St. Athanasios of Alexandria, spread monasticism throughout the Christian world. He reposed at a great age around the year 356, and is commemorated on January 17.
1-17.desc: Father of all monks and hermits.
1-17.name: Anthony the Great

1-17.bio:
St. George was a poor man from a village of Epirus who served as a groom in Ioannina. Accused by Muslims of having abandoned Islam, though he had always been a Christian, he refused every inducement to convert and was hanged in Ioannina in 1838.

His relics are venerated in the city, and he is one of the most beloved of the New Martyrs. He is commemorated on January 17.
1-17.desc: New Martyr George of Ioannina, martyred in 1838.
1-17.name: George of Ioannina

1-17.bio:
St. Anthony the New was born in Veria in Macedonia and lived as a hermit in a cave by the river Haliacmon, where tradition relates he spent many years in solitude and was granted the gift of miracles. His relics are venerated in Veria, of which he is the patron.

He is commemorated on January 17.
1-17.desc: Venerable Anthony the New, Wonderworker of Veria.
1-17.name: Anthony the New of Veria

1-17.bio:
St. Theodosios the Great was Roman emperor from 379 to 395. He established the Nicene faith as the faith of the empire, convened the Second Ecumenical Council at Constantinople in 381, and did public penance before St. Ambrose of Milan after the massacre at Thessaloniki.

He is commemorated on January 17.
1-17.desc: Holy Emperor Theodosios the Great, who convened the Second Ecumenical Council.
1-17.name: Theodosios the Great

1-17.bio:
St. Achillas was one of the desert fathers of Scetis in Egypt in the fourth and fifth centuries, whose sayings are preserved among those of the elders. He was known for the severity of his fasting and for his discretion toward the brethren.

He is commemorated on January 17.
1-17.desc: Venerable Achillas, an Egyptian desert father.
1-17.name: Achillas the Venerable

1-17.bio:
St. Anthony of Meteora, of the Kantakouzenos family according to tradition, was a monk of the Meteora in Thessaly in the fifteenth century, associated with the monastery of St. Stephen. He lived in asceticism on the rocks and reposed in peace.

He is commemorated on January 17.
1-17.name: Anthony of Meteora

1-18.bio:
St. Athanasios the Great, Archbishop of Alexandria, was born about the year 297 and as a young deacon accompanied his bishop to the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, where he stood against Arius in defense of the divinity of Christ. Made bishop of Alexandria in 328, he was driven into exile five times by Arian emperors yet never yielded, so that it was said of him: Athanasius against the world.

He wrote the Life of St. Anthony the Great, which spread monasticism throughout the Christian world, and many works in defense of the Orthodox faith. He reposed in peace in 373. Called the Father of Orthodoxy, he is commemorated together with St. Cyril of Alexandria on January 18, and on May 2 the translation of his relics is kept.
1-18.desc: Archbishop of Alexandria, Father of Orthodoxy, defender of Nicaea.
1-18.name: Athanasios the Great

1-18.bio:
St. Cyril was Archbishop of Alexandria in the fifth century. He presided at the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus in 431, which condemned Nestorius and confirmed that the Virgin Mary is truly Theotokos, the Mother of God.

A prolific theologian and commentator on Scripture, he reposed in 444. He is commemorated with St. Athanasios on January 18, and alone on June 9.
1-18.desc: St. Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria, champion of the title Theotokos.
1-18.name: Cyril of Alexandria

1-18.bio:
St. Theodoule was a Christian woman of Anazarbus in Cilicia who suffered in the persecution of Diocletian. Tradition relates that her steadfastness under torture led her tormentors Helladios, Evagrios, Makarios and Boethos to believe in Christ, and they were martyred with her.

She is commemorated on January 18.
1-18.desc: Holy Martyr Theodoule of Anazarbus and those who believed through her.
1-18.name: Theodoule the Martyr

1-18.bio:
St. Markianos was a nobleman of Cyrrhus in Syria in the fourth century who withdrew into the desert and enclosed himself in a small cell, living in silence and strict fasting. Disciples gathered around him, and his fame drew many visitors, whom he taught with wisdom.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 18.
1-18.desc: Venerable Markianos, hermit of the desert of Cyrrhus in Syria.
1-18.name: Markianos of Cyrrhus

1-18.bio:
St. Joachim was a monk of Mount Athos who returned to Bulgaria and founded a monastery on the river Danube. He was chosen as the first Patriarch of Trnovo after the restoration of the Bulgarian patriarchate in 1235 and governed the Church with holiness.

He reposed in 1246 and is commemorated on January 18.
1-18.desc: St. Joachim I, Patriarch of Trnovo and Bulgaria.
1-18.name: Joachim of Trnovo

1-19.bio:
St. Makarios of Egypt, called the Great, was one of the foremost of the desert fathers of the fourth century. Retiring to the desert of Scetis, he became the father of the monks who gathered there, renowned for his humility, his gentleness toward sinners, and his deep experience of prayer.

Many of his sayings are preserved among the words of the desert fathers, and spiritual homilies handed down under his name have nourished the Church for centuries. He reposed at a great age and is commemorated on January 19.
1-19.desc: Desert father and abbot of the Egyptian monks.
1-19.name: Makarios of Egypt

1-19.bio:
St. Makarios of Alexandria was a contemporary and friend of St. Makarios the Great. A merchant who was baptized in adulthood, he lived at the Cells in the Egyptian desert and became priest to the monks there, surpassing all in the severity of his ascetic feats.

He reposed in peace at a great age in the late fourth century. He is commemorated on January 19 together with St. Makarios of Egypt.
1-19.desc: Venerable Makarios of Alexandria, ascetic of the Cells.
1-19.name: Makarios of Alexandria

1-19.bio:
St. Mark Eugenikos was Metropolitan of Ephesus in the fifteenth century. At the Council of Ferrara-Florence he alone among the Greek bishops refused to sign the union with Rome, and his firmness, tradition relates, led the Pope to say that nothing had been accomplished.

Returning to Constantinople he strengthened the people in the Orthodox faith until his repose in 1444. He is commemorated on January 19.
1-19.desc: St. Mark of Ephesus, defender of Orthodoxy at the Council of Florence.
1-19.name: Mark Eugenikos

1-19.bio:
St. Arsenios was Archbishop of Corfu in the tenth century, a native of Bethany in Palestine according to tradition. He protected his flock, interceding with the emperor on their behalf, and composed hymns still used by the Church.

He reposed in peace and his relics are venerated in Corfu. He is commemorated on January 19.
1-19.desc: St. Arsenios, Archbishop of Corfu, hymnographer.
1-19.name: Arsenios of Corfu

1-19.bio:
St. Euphrasia was a Christian woman of noble family in Nicomedia during the persecution of Maximian. Refusing to sacrifice to the idols, she was handed over to a soldier to be dishonored; tradition relates that she preserved her chastity by a stratagem that cost her her life, being beheaded.

She is commemorated on January 19.
1-19.desc: Holy Virgin Martyr Euphrasia of Nicomedia.
1-19.name: Euphrasia of Nicomedia

1-19.bio:
St. Meletios was a monk of Mount Galesion near Ephesus in the thirteenth century. He opposed the union with Rome imposed by Michael VIII Palaiologos and for this was imprisoned, exiled, and had his tongue cut out.

He reposed in 1286 and is honored as a confessor. He is commemorated on January 19.
1-19.desc: Venerable Meletios the Confessor of Mount Galesion.
1-19.name: Meletios Galesiotes

1-2.bio:
St. Seraphim of Sarov, one of the most beloved saints of Russia, lived from the mid-eighteenth century until 1833. Entering the monastery of Sarov as a young man, he spent long years in seclusion in the forest in fasting, silence, and unceasing prayer, including, according to tradition, a thousand days and nights of prayer upon a rock.

In his last years he opened his cell to all, greeting every visitor as his joy with the paschal greeting that Christ is risen. Pilgrims beyond number received his counsel and healing. He taught that the aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit. His memory is kept on January 2.
1-2.desc: Beloved Russian monastic saint, wonderworker of Sarov.
1-2.name: Seraphim of Sarov

1-2.bio:
St. Sylvester was Bishop of Rome in the first half of the fourth century, during the reign of St. Constantine the Great, when the Church emerged from persecution. The First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea was held during his episcopate, and he was represented there by his legates.

Tradition connects him closely with the emperor Constantine and with the building of the first great churches of Rome. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 2.
1-2.desc: Pope of Rome in the time of St. Constantine the Great.
1-2.name: Sylvester of Rome

1-2.bio:
St. Theagenes was Bishop of Parium on the Hellespont. In the persecution under Licinius he was pressed to serve in the army and to deny Christ; refusing, he was imprisoned, tortured, and finally drowned in the sea.

Tradition relates that his relics were recovered by the faithful and became a source of healing. He is commemorated on January 2.
1-2.desc: Hieromartyr Theagenes, Bishop of Parium on the Hellespont.
1-2.name: Theagenes of Parium

1-2.bio:
St. Theodote was the mother of the Holy Unmercenaries Cosmas and Damian of Asia. Widowed young, she raised her sons in piety and in the fear of God, and it was from her that they learned the faith and the love of neighbor that marked their life of free healing.

She reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 2.
1-2.desc: Righteous Theodote, mother of the Holy Unmercenaries Cosmas and Damian.
1-2.name: Theodote the Mother of the Unmercenaries

1-2.bio:
St. Basil of Ancyra was a layman of that city who confessed Christ boldly during the reign of Julian the Apostate in the fourth century. Brought before the governor, he refused to sacrifice to the idols and was subjected to many tortures before being put to death.

He is commemorated on January 2.
1-2.desc: Holy Martyr Basil of Ancyra, who suffered under Julian the Apostate.
1-2.name: Basil of Ancyra

1-2.bio:
St. Juliana of Lazarevo was a Russian noblewoman of the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries who lived as a wife and mother near Murom. Without leaving the world, she gave herself to prayer and to unceasing works of mercy, feeding the hungry from her own table even during famine.

Her life was written by her son. She reposed in peace in 1604 and is commemorated on January 2.
1-2.desc: Righteous Juliana of Lazarevo, a laywoman of Murom famed for her mercy to the poor.
1-2.name: Juliana of Lazarevo

1-2.bio:
St. George the Iberian, called Zorzis, was a Georgian by birth who had been taken captive and forced to embrace Islam as a child. Tradition relates that as an adult in Mytilene he returned openly to the Christian faith and, refusing to deny Christ, was hanged in 1770.

He is numbered among the New Martyrs and is commemorated on January 2.
1-2.desc: New Martyr George of Georgia, martyred at Mytilene in the eighteenth century.
1-2.name: George the Iberian

1-20.bio:
St. Euthymios the Great was born in Melitene of Armenia in the fourth century and became one of the great fathers of the Palestinian desert. Settling in the wilderness east of Jerusalem, he founded a famous lavra, guided multitudes of monks, and formed disciples who themselves became pillars of monasticism, among them St. Savas the Sanctified.

A staunch defender of the Orthodox faith of the Council of Chalcedon, he reposed at a very great age in the fifth century. He is commemorated on January 20.
1-20.desc: Great monastic father of the Palestinian desert.
1-20.name: Euthymios the Great

1-20.bio:
St. Zacharias was a furrier from Arta who in his youth had embraced Islam. Repenting, he returned to Christ, went to Patras, and there openly confessed his faith before the judge; after torture he was put to death in 1782.

He is commemorated on January 20.
1-20.desc: New Martyr Zacharias of Arta, martyred at Patras.
1-20.name: Zacharias of Arta

1-20.bio:
Sts. Bassos, Eusebios, Eutychios and Basilides were men of senatorial rank in Nicomedia who, tradition relates, believed in Christ on witnessing the martyrdom of Bishop Theopemptos. They were subjected to various tortures and put to death in the persecution of Diocletian.

They are commemorated on January 20.
1-20.desc: Holy Martyrs of Nicomedia, senators converted by the martyrdom of St. Theopemptos.
1-20.name: Bassos, Eusebios, Eutychios and Basilides

1-20.bio:
Sts. Innas, Pinnas and Rimmas were natives of Scythia, north of the Black Sea, and according to tradition disciples of the Apostle Andrew. Having preached Christ among the pagans, they were bound to stakes in a frozen river and died of the cold.

They are commemorated on January 20.
1-20.desc: Holy Martyrs of Scythia, disciples of the Apostle Andrew.
1-20.name: Innas, Pinnas and Rimmas

1-20.bio:
St. Peter was a hard-hearted tax-collector in Africa in the sixth century who, tradition relates, once threw a loaf of bread at a beggar in anger and saw in a vision that even this was counted to him as alms. Converted, he gave all his goods to the poor and sold himself into slavery to serve the needy.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 20.
1-20.desc: Blessed Peter the Tax-Collector, who was converted through almsgiving.
1-20.name: Peter the Publican

1-20.bio:
St. Leo I was Byzantine emperor from 457 to 474, a Thracian by birth. Tradition relates that he was granted a vision of the Theotokos at the spring outside Constantinople, where he built the church of the Life-Giving Spring; he was also a benefactor of the poor and of the Church.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 20.
1-20.desc: Holy Emperor Leo I the Great, called Makelles, of Thrace.
1-20.name: Leo the Great the Emperor

1-20.bio:
St. Euthymios was a disciple of St. Theodosios of Trnovo and lived for a time on Mount Athos before becoming Patriarch of Trnovo in 1375. A learned hesychast, he reformed the Slavonic liturgical books and strengthened his flock during the Ottoman conquest, after which he was exiled.

He reposed around 1402 and is commemorated on January 20.
1-20.desc: St. Euthymios, Patriarch of Trnovo, teacher of the Bulgarian people.
1-20.name: Euthymios of Trnovo

1-21.bio:
St. Maximos the Confessor was a monk and theologian of the seventh century. Leaving high office in Constantinople for the monastic life, he became the great champion of the truth that Christ, being true God and true man, possesses both a divine and a human will, standing almost alone against the Monothelite heresy supported by emperor and patriarch.

For his confession he was tried, mutilated, and exiled, dying in banishment; the Church soon vindicated his teaching. His profound writings on the spiritual life are treasured to this day. He is commemorated on January 21.
1-21.desc: Theologian and confessor who defended Orthodoxy.
1-21.name: Maximos the Confessor

1-21.bio:
St. Neophytos was born in Nicaea and from childhood was distinguished by prayer and wonders; tradition relates that at ten he lived in a cave on Mount Olympus. In the persecution of Diocletian, at the age of fifteen, he confessed Christ before the governor, was tortured, and was pierced with a spear.

He is commemorated on January 21.
1-21.desc: Holy Martyr Neophytos of Nicaea, a youth martyred at fifteen.
1-21.name: Neophytos the Martyr

1-21.bio:
St. Agnes was a young girl of Rome who, refusing marriage for love of Christ, was denounced as a Christian in the persecution of the early fourth century. Tradition relates that she was sent to a brothel and preserved unharmed by God before being put to death by the sword at the age of about thirteen.

She is commemorated on January 21.
1-21.desc: Holy Virgin Martyr Agnes of Rome.
1-21.name: Agnes of Rome

1-21.bio:
St. Maximos the Greek was born in Arta in 1470, studied in Italy, and became a monk at Vatopedi on Mount Athos. Sent to Moscow to translate sacred books, he was falsely accused, condemned, and kept in confinement for many years, which he bore with patience.

He reposed in 1556 at the Holy Trinity Lavra. He is commemorated on January 21.
1-21.desc: Venerable Maximos the Greek, Athonite scholar and confessor in Russia.
1-21.name: Maximos the Greek

1-21.bio:
Sts. Eugenios, Candidus, Valerian and Aquila were Christians of Trebizond in the persecution of Diocletian. Tradition relates that Eugenios overthrew the idol of Mithras on the mountain above the city; the four were arrested, tortured, and beheaded.

St. Eugenios is the patron of Trebizond and is greatly honored by the Greeks of Pontus. They are commemorated on January 21.
1-21.desc: Holy Martyrs Eugenios, Candidus, Valerian and Aquila of Trebizond.
1-21.name: Eugenios of Trebizond and those with him

1-21.bio:
St. Patroklos was a wealthy Christian of Troyes in Gaul who devoted his goods to the poor. In the persecution of the third century he confessed Christ before the governor and was beheaded.

He is commemorated on January 21.
1-21.name: Patroklos the Martyr

1-21.bio:
St. Zosimas was given by his parents to a monastery in Sicily as a child and grew up in the monastic life, later becoming abbot. In the seventh century he was made Bishop of Syracuse, where he cared for the poor and reposed in peace.

He is commemorated on January 21.
1-21.name: Zosimas of Syracuse

1-22.bio:
St. Timothy the Apostle was the beloved disciple and fellow worker of St. Paul, who called him his true child in the faith. A native of Lystra, born of a Greek father and a devout Jewish mother, he accompanied Paul on his journeys and received from him the two epistles that bear his name. He served as the first Bishop of Ephesus.

According to tradition he ended his life as a martyr in Ephesus, struck down by pagans whose idolatrous festival he had rebuked. He is commemorated on January 22.
1-22.desc: Holy Apostle Timothy, disciple of Paul.
1-22.name: Timothy the Apostle

1-22.bio:
St. Anastasios was a Persian soldier who, tradition relates, was drawn to Christ when the True Cross was carried to Persia after the sack of Jerusalem in 614. Baptized in Jerusalem, he became a monk; returning to Persia he was arrested, tortured, and strangled in 628.

His relics were later brought to Constantinople and Rome. He is commemorated on January 22.
1-22.desc: Venerable Martyr Anastasios the Persian, a soldier converted by the Precious Cross.
1-22.name: Anastasios the Persian

1-22.bio:
In the ninth century, during the wars between Byzantium and the Bulgarian khan Krum and his successors, the bishops Manuel of Adrianople, George of Develtos, Peter and Leo, together with clergy, soldiers and a great multitude of Christian captives numbering 377, were put to death for refusing to deny Christ.

They are commemorated on January 22.
1-22.desc: Bishops Manuel, George, Peter and Leo and 377 companions, martyred in Bulgaria.
1-22.name: Martyrs of Bulgaria under Manuel and George

1-22.bio:
St. Joseph the Sanctified was born in Crete in the fifteenth century and became a monk near Heraklion, giving himself to prayer and charity. He reposed in 1511, and his incorrupt relics were later carried to Zakynthos, where they are venerated.

He is commemorated on January 22.
1-22.desc: Venerable Joseph the Sanctified, a monk of Crete whose relics rest in Zakynthos.
1-22.name: Joseph the Sanctified of Samaka

1-22.bio:
St. Vissarion Korkoliakos was a monk of the Agathonos Monastery near Ypati in central Greece in the twentieth century, known for his simplicity, prayer, and charity to the poor. He reposed in 1991, and his relics were found incorrupt.

He was glorified as a saint by the Ecumenical Patriarchate and is commemorated on January 22.
1-22.desc: Venerable Vissarion Korkoliakos of the Agathonos Monastery.
1-22.name: Vissarion of Agathonos

1-23.bio:
St. Clement was Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, in Asia Minor, during the great persecutions at the turn of the fourth century. Tradition relates that he endured an extraordinarily long martyrdom, suffering imprisonments and tortures over many years in city after city, yet never wavering in his confession of Christ.

With him is honored the martyr Agathangelos, who shared his bonds and his sufferings. Clement finished his course by the sword, receiving the crown he had so long awaited. They are commemorated on January 23.
1-23.name: Clement of Ankyra

1-23.bio:
St. Agathangelos was a Roman who was baptized by St. Clement of Ankyra and became his companion in the long years of his sufferings. Together they endured tortures in many cities before being beheaded at Ankyra in the early fourth century.

He is commemorated with St. Clement on January 23.
1-23.desc: Holy Martyr Agathangelos, companion of St. Clement of Ankyra.
1-23.name: Agathangelos the Martyr

1-23.bio:
St. Dionysios was born in Thessaly and became a monk on Mount Athos, where he was abbot of Philotheou. He later withdrew to Mount Olympus in Macedonia and founded there the monastery of the Holy Trinity that bears his name.

He reposed in 1541 and is greatly venerated in Macedonia and Thessaly. He is commemorated on January 23.
1-23.desc: Venerable Dionysios of Olympus, founder of the monastery on Mount Olympus.
1-23.name: Dionysios of Olympus

1-23.bio:
St. Acholios was Bishop of Thessaloniki in the fourth century. He baptized the Emperor Theodosios the Great in that city in 380, and was praised by St. Ambrose of Milan for his holiness.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 23.
1-23.desc: St. Acholios, Bishop of Thessaloniki, who baptized Emperor Theodosios the Great.
1-23.name: Acholios of Thessaloniki

1-23.bio:
St. Salamanes lived in a small cell on the bank of the Euphrates in the fourth century, keeping complete silence and receiving no visitors. Tradition relates that the people of his native village carried him off to have him among them, and that he remained silent and untroubled throughout.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 23.
1-23.desc: Venerable Salamanes the Hesychast of the Euphrates.
1-23.name: Salamanes the Silent

1-23.bio:
St. Mausimas was a priest in a village near Cyrrhus in Syria in the fourth century, who lived in extreme poverty and gave everything to the poor. Tradition relates that his jar of oil and bin of grain never ran out, however much he gave away.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 23.
1-23.desc: Venerable Mausimas the Syrian, a priest and ascetic.
1-23.name: Mausimas the Syrian

1-24.bio:
Blessed Xenia of St. Petersburg lived in the eighteenth century. Widowed at twenty-six when her husband died suddenly, she gave away her possessions, put on his military coat, and took up the ascetic path of the fool-for-Christ, wandering the streets of the city for some forty-five years, praying at night in the fields and secretly helping the poor.

The people came to revere her as a woman of God, and her prayers were sought for healing, for families, and for those in need. She is invoked especially for help in finding work, housing, and a spouse. The Church commemorates her on January 24.
1-24.desc: Blessed Xenia of St. Petersburg, fool-for-Christ.
1-24.name: Xenia of Petersburg

1-24.bio:
St. Xenia was born in Rome in the fifth century to a family of rank and was named Eusebia. Fleeing an arranged marriage with two of her maidservants, she took the name Xenia, meaning stranger, and settled at Mylasa in Caria, where she founded a convent and lived in great humility.

Tradition relates that a cross of stars appeared in the sky at her repose. She is commemorated on January 24.
1-24.desc: Venerable Xenia of Rome and her two maidservants.
1-24.name: Xenia of Rome

1-24.bio:
St. Neophytos was born in Cyprus in 1134 and, after failing to reach the hermits of Mount Latros, carved a cell for himself in a cliff near Paphos, where he lived as a recluse for nearly fifty years. A community gathered around him, and he wrote many spiritual works.

His cave and monastery, the Enkleistra, remain a place of pilgrimage. He is commemorated on January 24.
1-24.desc: Venerable Neophytos the Recluse of Cyprus.
1-24.name: Neophytos the Recluse

1-24.bio:
St. Babylas was a priest who left his home in the East for Sicily, where he lived in asceticism with his disciples Timothy and Agapios and drew many to Christ. Tradition relates that pagans seized the three and put them to death.

They are commemorated on January 24.
1-24.desc: Hieromartyr Babylas of Sicily and his disciples Timothy and Agapios.
1-24.name: Babylas of Sicily

1-24.bio:
St. Philon was a deacon whom St. Epiphanios of Cyprus ordained Bishop of Karpasia in the fourth century. He was granted the gift of miracles and wrote a commentary on the Song of Songs.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 24.
1-24.desc: St. Philon the Wonderworker, Bishop of Karpasia in Cyprus.
1-24.name: Philon of Karpasia

1-24.bio:
St. Makedonios lived for many decades on the mountains of Syria in the fourth and fifth centuries, eating only barley and later a little bread, and was called the Barley-Eater. Tradition relates that he healed the sick and interceded for the people of Antioch after their revolt against the emperor.

He reposed in peace at a great age and is commemorated on January 24.
1-24.desc: Venerable Makedonios the Hermit of Syria.
1-24.name: Makedonios the Hermit

1-25.bio:
St. Gregory the Theologian was born in Cappadocia in the fourth century and studied in Athens with his close friend St. Basil the Great. A man of deep prayer and unmatched eloquence, he was called to Constantinople when the city was dominated by Arianism, and through his celebrated theological orations restored the Orthodox faith in the Holy Trinity. He briefly served as Archbishop of Constantinople before withdrawing to a life of quiet and asceticism.

The Church has given the title Theologian only to him, to St. John the Evangelist, and to St. Symeon the New Theologian. One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, he is commemorated on January 25.
1-25.desc: Archbishop of Constantinople, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs.
1-25.name: Gregory the Theologian

1-25.bio:
St. Auxentios was born in Bella in Epirus and worked as a furrier in Constantinople. Having once in fear spoken words of denial, he repented and, after preparing himself with the guidance of his confessor, went before the judge, confessed Christ, and was beheaded in 1720.

He is commemorated on January 25.
1-25.desc: New Martyr Auxentios of Bella, martyred in Constantinople.
1-25.name: Auxentios the New Martyr

1-25.bio:
St. Publius was a senator's son of Zeugma on the Euphrates in the fourth century who sold his goods for the poor and founded a monastic community on a hill near the city, gathering both Greek- and Syriac-speaking monks.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 25.
1-25.desc: Venerable Publius of Syria, founder of a monastery near Zeugma.
1-25.name: Publius the Ascetic

1-25.bio:
St. Kastinos was a Roman of senatorial rank who, tradition relates, was healed and converted by St. Cyprian of Carthage and became Bishop of Byzantium in the third century, before the city became Constantinople.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 25.
1-25.name: Kastinos of Byzantium

1-25.bio:
St. Bretannion was Bishop of Tomis on the Black Sea, in present-day Romania, in the fourth century. When the Arian emperor Valens visited and tried to force his heresy on the Church, the bishop led his flock out of the cathedral rather than commune with him.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 25.
1-25.desc: St. Bretannion, Bishop of Tomis in Scythia Minor.
1-25.name: Bretannion of Tomis

1-25.bio:
St. Anatole was a disciple of the elders Makarios and Ambrose of Optina in the nineteenth century and later a spiritual father of the Optina skete and of the convent at Shamordino. He was a teacher of the Jesus Prayer and of humility.

He reposed in 1894 and is commemorated on January 25.
1-25.desc: Venerable Anatole the Elder of Optina.
1-25.name: Anatole of Optina

1-25.bio:
St. Vladimir was Metropolitan of Kiev and had earlier served as Metropolitan of Moscow and of St. Petersburg. In January 1918 he was seized by armed men at the Kiev Caves Lavra, led outside its walls, and shot, becoming the first bishop to suffer under the Bolsheviks.

He is commemorated on January 25 and with the New Martyrs of Russia.
1-25.desc: Hieromartyr Vladimir, Metropolitan of Kiev, first of the Russian New Martyrs.
1-25.name: Vladimir of Kiev

1-26.bio:
St. Xenophon was a devout and wealthy man of Constantinople in the sixth century, who with his wife Mary raised their two sons, Arkadios and John, in the fear of God. When the young men were shipwrecked on a voyage to their studies, each was saved without the other's knowledge, and each in gratitude took up the monastic life in the Holy Land.

Seeking their sons, Xenophon and Mary found them by God's providence, and the whole family gave itself to Christ in monasticism. They are commemorated together on January 26.
1-26.desc: Venerable Xenophon and Mary of Constantinople.
1-26.name: Xenophon

1-26.bio:
St. Symeon the Ancient lived as a hermit in a cave on Mount Amanus in Syria in the fourth century, and later founded a monastery there. Tradition relates that wild beasts served him and that he made a pilgrimage to Mount Sinai.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 26.
1-26.desc: Venerable Symeon the Ancient, hermit of Mount Amanus.
1-26.name: Symeon the Ancient

1-26.bio:
St. Ammonas was a disciple of St. Anthony the Great and, after the saint's repose, guided his disciples in the Egyptian desert. His letters on the spiritual life are preserved, and his sayings appear among those of the Desert Fathers.

He reposed in peace in the fourth century and is commemorated on January 26.
1-26.desc: Venerable Ammonas, disciple of St. Anthony the Great.
1-26.name: Ammonas the Venerable

1-26.bio:
St. Clement lived as an ascetic on Mount Sagmata in Boeotia, where the monastery of the Transfiguration was later established. Tradition relates that he lived on a pillar and drew disciples by his holiness; his relics are venerated at the monastery.

He is commemorated on January 26.
1-26.desc: Venerable Clement the Ascetic of Mount Sagmata in Boeotia.
1-26.name: Clement of Sagmata

1-26.bio:
St. Ananias was a priest in Phoenicia during the persecution of Diocletian. Brought before the governor, he refused to sacrifice; tradition relates that his jailer Peter and seven soldiers believed in Christ at the sight of his sufferings and were drowned in the sea with him.

They are commemorated on January 26.
1-26.desc: Holy Martyrs Ananias the Presbyter, Peter the jailer, and seven soldiers of Phoenicia.
1-26.greek: Ανανίας, Πέτρος και οι επτά στρατιώτες
1-26.name: Ananias, Peter and the Seven Soldiers

1-26.bio:
St. David IV, called the Builder, was king of Georgia from 1089 to 1125. He freed his land from the Seljuk Turks, restored the churches and monasteries, founded the Gelati Monastery and academy, and was famed for his humility and his Hymns of Repentance.

He is commemorated on January 26.
1-26.desc: Holy King David IV the Builder of Georgia.
1-26.name: David the Builder

1-26.bio:
St. Theodore the Studite, abbot of the Studion Monastery and confessor for the holy icons, died in exile in 826. In 844, after the restoration of the icons, his relics and those of his brother St. Joseph of Thessaloniki were solemnly returned to the Studion.

The translation is commemorated on January 26; his main feast is November 11.
1-26.desc: Translation of the relics of St. Theodore the Studite to Constantinople.
1-26.name: Translation of the Relics of Theodore the Studite

1-27.bio:
St. John Chrysostom, the Golden-Mouthed, was born in Antioch in the fourth century. First a monk and then a priest famed for his preaching, he was taken to Constantinople and consecrated its Archbishop. He preached constantly on the Scriptures, gave generously to the poor, and fearlessly rebuked the luxury and injustice of the powerful, for which he was twice driven into exile, dying with words of thanksgiving, glorifying God for all things.

The Divine Liturgy most often served in the Orthodox Church bears his name. One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, he is commemorated on January 27, the return of his relics to Constantinople, and again on November 13.
1-27.name: John Chrysostom

1-27.bio:
St. Markiane was an empress of Constantinople remembered for her piety and charity, identified by tradition with the wife of the Emperor Justin. The synaxaria record that she reposed in peace after a life of good works.

She is commemorated on January 27.
1-27.name: Markiane the Empress

1-27.bio:
St. Peter the Egyptian was a disciple of Abba Lot in the Egyptian desert in the fifth century, whose sayings are preserved among those of the Desert Fathers. He was known for his extreme poverty and fasting.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 27.
1-27.desc: Venerable Peter the Egyptian, disciple of Abba Lot.
1-27.name: Peter the Egyptian

1-27.bio:
St. Demetrios was a young Christian of Galata in Constantinople who, tradition relates, was falsely accused of insulting Islam after a quarrel and, refusing to convert, was beheaded in 1784.

He is commemorated on January 27.
1-27.name: Demetrios of Constantinople

1-27.bio:
St. Demetrianos was Bishop of Tamassos in Cyprus, remembered in the island as a wonderworker. Little is recorded of his life beyond the tradition of his holiness and the miracles worked through his prayers.

He is commemorated on January 27.
1-27.desc: St. Demetrianos the Wonderworker, Bishop of Tamassos in Cyprus.
1-27.name: Demetrianos of Tamassos

1-27.bio:
St. Ashot Kuropalates was a Georgian prince of the ninth century who ruled in Tao-Klarjeti, restored the churches and monasteries of the region, and supported St. Gregory of Khandzta. Tradition relates that he was murdered in a church.

He is commemorated on January 27.
1-27.desc: Holy King Ashot Kuropalates of Georgia.
1-27.name: Ashot the King

1-28.bio:
St. Ephrem the Syrian was born in Nisibis in Mesopotamia early in the fourth century and later settled in Edessa. A deacon who out of humility refused higher office, he became the greatest hymnographer of the Syriac church, called the Harp of the Holy Spirit, and his hymns and homilies taught the faith to generations.

A man of deep compunction, he wrote constantly of repentance, and the Lenten prayer that bears his name is offered throughout the Great Fast in every Orthodox church. He reposed in 373 and is commemorated on January 28.
1-28.desc: Poet, theologian and hymn-writer of the Syrian church.
1-28.name: Ephrem the Syrian

1-28.bio:
St. Palladios lived as a hermit in a cell on a mountain near Antioch in the fourth century, spending his days in prayer and labor. Tradition relates that a murdered merchant was left at his door and that through his prayer the dead man revealed the true killer.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 28.
1-28.desc: Venerable Palladios the Hermit of Syria.
1-28.name: Palladios of Antioch

1-28.bio:
St. James lived as a hermit near Porphyreon in Phoenicia in the sixth century and was granted the gift of healing. Tradition relates that he fell into grave sin and, despairing, nearly abandoned his repentance, but was restored through counsel and years of penance in a tomb, and again received the grace of God.

He is commemorated on January 28.
1-28.desc: Venerable James the Ascetic of Porphyreon, who repented of grave sin.
1-28.name: James the Ascetic

1-28.bio: St. Charis is commemorated on January 28 as a holy woman martyr. The synaxaria record that she ended her contest for Christ, but the details of her life have not been preserved.
1-28.name: Charis the Martyr

1-28.bio:
St. Isaac the Syrian lived in the seventh century and was for a short time Bishop of Nineveh before withdrawing to the solitary life in the mountains. His ascetical homilies, translated into Greek by the monks of St. Sabbas, became one of the most treasured spiritual books of the Orthodox Church.

He is commemorated on January 28 together with St. Ephrem the Syrian.
1-28.desc: St. Isaac the Syrian, Bishop of Nineveh, teacher of the spiritual life.
1-28.name: Isaac the Syrian

1-28.bio:
St. Theodosios was a monk of Vologda in the sixteenth century who founded the monastery of the Savior at Totma, laboring in humility and strictness. He reposed in 1568, and his relics were later found incorrupt.

He is commemorated on January 28.
1-28.desc: Venerable Theodosios of Totma, founder of the Spaso-Sumorin Monastery.
1-28.name: Theodosios of Totma

1-28.bio:
St. Ephraim was a Hungarian by birth who served the holy princes Boris and Gleb. After the murder of his brother George with St. Boris, he became a monk and founded a monastery and hospice at Novy Torg, where he reposed in the eleventh century.

He is commemorated on January 28.
1-28.desc: Venerable Ephraim the Wonderworker of Novy Torg.
1-28.name: Ephraim of Novy Torg

1-29.bio:
St. Ignatios the God-Bearer was Bishop of Antioch and one of the apostolic fathers, a disciple of the apostles themselves. Condemned under the Emperor Trajan at the beginning of the second century, he was taken in bonds to Rome and given to the wild beasts in the arena, going to his death with joy, longing, as he wrote, to be ground as the wheat of God.

The seven epistles he wrote on that final journey remain treasures of the early Church. On January 29 the Church commemorates the translation of his relics; his martyrdom is kept on December 20.
1-29.desc: Bishop of Antioch and apostolic father.
1-29.name: Ignatios the God-Bearer

1-29.bio:
St. Demetrios was born in Chios and worked in Constantinople. Tradition relates that he was falsely accused of promising to become a Muslim, and that refusing to do so he was beheaded in 1802.

He is commemorated on January 29.
1-29.desc: New Martyr Demetrios of Chios, martyred in Constantinople.
1-29.name: Demetrios of Chios

1-29.bio:
Sts. Romanos, James, Philotheos, Hyperechios, Abibos, Julian and Paregorios were Christians of Samosata on the Euphrates who refused to take part in pagan sacrifices during the persecution of Maximian. After torture they were put to death by nails driven into their heads.

They are commemorated on January 29.
1-29.desc: Holy Martyrs Romanos, James, Philotheos, Hyperechios, Abibos, Julian and Paregorios of Samosata.
1-29.name: Seven Martyrs of Samosata

1-29.bio:
St. Sarbelos was a pagan priest of Edessa who, together with his sister Bebaia, was converted to Christ by the bishop St. Barsimaios. In the persecution of Trajan the two confessed the faith and were put to death.

They are commemorated on January 29.
1-29.desc: Holy Martyrs Sarbelos and his sister Bebaia of Edessa.
1-29.name: Sarbelos and Bebaia

1-29.bio:
St. Aphraates was a Persian who came to Edessa and then to Antioch in the fourth century and lived as a hermit. He defended the Orthodox faith against the Arians in the reign of Valens, and tradition relates that he answered the emperor's rebuke with the boldness of a father of the Church.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 29.
1-29.desc: Venerable Aphraates the Persian, ascetic of Antioch.
1-29.name: Aphraates the Persian

1-29.bio:
St. Andrei Rublev was a monk of the Holy Trinity Lavra and of the Andronikov Monastery in Moscow in the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries, the greatest of the Russian iconographers. His icon of the Holy Trinity is honored as the model of Orthodox iconography.

He reposed around 1430 and is commemorated on January 29.
1-29.name: Andrei Rublev

1-29.bio:
St. Silvanos was Bishop of Emesa in Syria for forty years. In the persecution under Maximian he was arrested with his deacon Luke and the reader Mokios; after imprisonment the three were given to wild beasts in the amphitheater.

They are commemorated on January 29.
1-29.desc: Hieromartyr Silvanos, Bishop of Emesa, with Luke the deacon and Mokios the reader.
1-29.name: Silvanos, Luke and Mokios

1-3.bio:
St. Gordios was a centurion of Caesarea in Cappadocia who lived in the time of the persecutions of the early fourth century. Withdrawing to the wilderness to live in prayer, he returned to the city during a great pagan festival and openly confessed Christ before the assembled crowds, knowing the cost. He was condemned and beheaded for his confession.

St. Basil the Great, a later bishop of the same city, honored his memory with a celebrated homily, and the Church has kept his name ever since as a model of fearless witness. He is commemorated on January 3.
1-3.name: Gordios

1-3.bio:
The Holy Prophet Malachi is the last of the twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament. His name means messenger of the Lord, and his book, written after the return from the Babylonian captivity, calls the priests and people back to faithful worship.

He foretold the coming of the Forerunner and the day of the Lord. He is commemorated on January 3.
1-3.desc: Holy Prophet Malachi, last of the twelve minor prophets.
1-3.name: Malachi the Prophet

1-3.bio:
St. Thomais was born on the island of Lesbos and lived in Constantinople in the tenth century. Married to a harsh and violent husband, she bore his ill-treatment with patience and gave herself to prayer, fasting, and generous almsgiving.

After her repose her tomb became a place of healing. She is commemorated on January 3.
1-3.desc: Righteous Thomais of Lesbos, a married woman of Constantinople renowned for patience and almsgiving.
1-3.name: Thomais of Lesbos

1-3.bio:
St. Genevieve lived in Gaul in the fifth century and was consecrated to God from childhood. Tradition relates that she encouraged the people of Paris to stand firm through prayer and fasting when the Huns threatened the city, and that it was spared.

She lived a long life of asceticism and charity and is honored as the patroness of Paris. She is commemorated on January 3.
1-3.name: Genevieve of Paris

1-3.bio:
St. Peter of Atroa was a monk and abbot in Bithynia in the ninth century, called the Sign-Bearer because of the many miracles worked through his prayers. He lived through the iconoclast persecution, defending the veneration of the holy icons.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 3.
1-3.desc: Venerable Peter the Sign-Bearer, abbot of the monastery of St. Zacharias at Atroa.
1-3.name: Peter of Atroa

1-3.bio: St. Akakios the Wonderworker is commemorated on January 3 as a monastic father who, tradition relates, was granted the gift of miracles and served as abbot of his community. Few details of his life have been preserved beyond the record of his holiness.
1-3.desc: Venerable Akakios the Wonderworker, an ascetic and abbot.
1-3.name: Akakios the Wonderworker

1-3.bio:
St. Ephraim of Nea Makri was a monk of the Monastery of the Annunciation on Mount Amomon in Attica, martyred there by Turkish raiders in the fifteenth century. His relics were discovered on January 3, 1950, after the abbess of the restored monastery was led to their place through prayer.

Since their finding he has become one of the most beloved wonderworking saints of modern Greece. His martyrdom is kept on May 5, and the finding of his relics on January 3.
1-3.desc: Commemoration of the finding of the relics of St. Ephraim the New Martyr at Nea Makri.
1-3.name: Finding of the Relics of Ephraim of Nea Makri

1-30.bio:
St. Hippolytos was a martyr of the Church of Rome who gave his life for Christ during the persecutions of the third century. The synaxaria preserve little of his story beyond his faithful confession and his death for the Lord, in company with other martyrs of that city.

His memory has been kept from ancient times among the witnesses of the Roman Church, whose blood became the seed of the faith. He is commemorated on January 30.
1-30.name: Hippolytos

1-30.bio:
The feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs honors together Sts. Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom, the great fathers and ecumenical teachers of the Church. According to tradition, the common feast was established in the eleventh century after disputes arose in Constantinople over which of the three was greatest; the hierarchs made known in a vision that they are one before God, and a shared commemoration was appointed.

Together they represent the harmony of theology, eloquence, and pastoral care. In Greece the day is also kept as the feast of education and letters, the patronal celebration of schools, teachers, and students.
1-30.desc: Feast of Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom.
1-30.name: Three Holy Hierarchs

1-30.bio:
St. Chryse was a Christian maiden of Rome in the third century who, tradition relates, had been exiled for her faith and lived at Ostia, where she encouraged the confessors imprisoned there. She was tortured and drowned in the sea with a stone about her neck.

She is commemorated on January 30 together with St. Hippolytos and those with him.
1-30.desc: Holy Virgin Martyr Chryse of Rome, who suffered with St. Hippolytos.
1-30.name: Chryse the Martyr

1-30.bio:
Sts. Kensourinos, a Roman magistrate, and Sabinos were among those who confessed Christ at Ostia in the third century together with St. Hippolytos and St. Chryse. Tradition relates that Kensourinos believed after seeing a dead man raised through the prayers of a Christian priest, and was beheaded.

They are commemorated on January 30.
1-30.desc: Holy Martyrs Kensourinos and Sabinos, who suffered with St. Hippolytos at Ostia.
1-30.name: Kensourinos and Sabinos

1-30.bio:
St. Theophilos the New was a commander of the Byzantine forces in Cyprus in the eighth century. Captured by the Arabs, he was held for years in prison and, refusing to deny Christ, was beheaded around 792.

He is commemorated on January 30.
1-30.desc: Holy Martyr Theophilos the New, a Byzantine commander martyred by the Arabs.
1-30.name: Theophilos the New

1-30.bio:
St. Theodore was a Christian of Mytilene who had in a moment of weakness embraced Islam. Repenting, he returned openly to Christ, confessed his faith before the judge, and was hanged in Mytilene in 1784.

He is commemorated on January 30.
1-30.desc: New Martyr Theodore Hatzis of Mytilene.
1-30.name: Theodore Hatzis of Mytilene

1-30.bio:
On January 30, 1823, after visions granted to the nun St. Pelagia of Tinos, the wonderworking icon of the Annunciation of the Theotokos was found buried in a field on the island of Tinos. The great church of the Evangelistria was built over the spot, and the island became the foremost place of pilgrimage in Greece.

The finding of the icon is commemorated on January 30.
1-30.desc: Commemoration of the finding of the wonderworking icon of the Annunciation on Tinos.
1-30.name: Finding of the Icon of the Annunciation in Tinos

1-30.bio:
St. Pelagia was a married woman of Arzamas who, with the blessing of St. Seraphim of Sarov, took up the life of a fool-for-Christ and lived at the Diveyevo convent, enduring beatings and mockery with patience. She was granted the gifts of clairvoyance and healing.

She reposed in 1884 and is commemorated on January 30.
1-30.name: Pelagia of Diveyevo

1-31.bio:
Sts. Cyrus and John are honored among the Holy Unmercenaries, physicians who healed in the name of Christ without accepting payment. Cyrus was a physician of Alexandria and John a soldier who joined him; together they served the sick and strengthened the persecuted during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century.

Hastening to encourage a Christian woman and her daughters under arrest, they were themselves seized, confessed Christ, and were beheaded. The faithful have long sought their intercession for healing. They are commemorated on January 31.
1-31.name: Cyrus and John

1-31.bio:
St. Athanasia was a Christian woman of Canopus in Egypt who was arrested with her three daughters, Theoktiste, Theodote and Eudoxia, in the persecution of Diocletian. The Unmercenaries Cyrus and John came to strengthen them and were arrested too; after torture all were beheaded.

They are commemorated on January 31.
1-31.desc: Holy Martyr Athanasia with her daughters Theoktiste, Theodote and Eudoxia, martyred with Sts. Cyrus and John.
1-31.name: Athanasia and her Daughters

1-31.bio:
St. Arsenios was born in Ioannina in 1800 and became a monk on Mount Athos before settling in the Cyclades. He served as spiritual father of the convent of the Transfiguration on Paros, where he was famed for his prayer, discernment, and miracles.

He reposed in 1877, and his relics are venerated on Paros. He is commemorated on January 31.
1-31.desc: Venerable Arsenios the New of Paros, wonderworker.
1-31.name: Arsenios of Paros

1-31.bio:
Sts. Victorinus, Victor, Nikephoros, Claudius, Diodorus, Serapion and Papias were Christians of Corinth who confessed Christ in the persecution of Decius and, after being sent to Egypt, were put to death by various cruel tortures.

They are commemorated on January 31.
1-31.desc: Holy Martyrs Victorinus, Victor, Nikephoros, Claudius, Diodorus, Serapion and Papias of Corinth.
1-31.greek: Ουικτωρίνος, Ουίκτωρ και οι συν αυτοίς
1-31.name: Victorinus, Victor and those with them

1-31.bio:
St. Tryphaina was a Christian woman of Cyzicus who openly rebuked the pagans and confessed Christ. Tradition relates that she was cast to wild beasts and remained unharmed until a bull gored her.

She is commemorated on January 31.
1-31.name: Tryphaina of Cyzicus

1-31.bio:
St. Elias Ardounis was a barber of Kalamata who had embraced Islam and later repented, becoming a monk on Mount Athos. Returning to Kalamata, he publicly confessed Christ and was burned alive in 1686.

He is commemorated on January 31.
1-31.desc: New Monk-Martyr Elias Ardounis of Kalamata.
1-31.name: Elias Ardounis

1-4.bio:
St. Anastasia was a holy woman and martyr of Rome who gave her life for Christ during the persecutions of the early Church. The synaxaria preserve little of her story beyond her faithful confession, but her name, which means resurrection, has been cherished by the faithful as a sign of the hope for which she died.

Her endurance joins her to the great company of women martyrs whom the Church honors as brides of Christ. Her memory is kept on January 4.
1-4.name: Anastasia

1-4.bio:
The Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles gathers into one feast all those disciples whom the Lord sent out two by two before Him, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke, together with the fellow-workers of the Twelve named in the Epistles.

Each of the Seventy also has his own day of commemoration through the year; on January 4 the Church honors them all together.
1-4.desc: Joint commemoration of the Seventy Apostles sent out by the Lord.
1-4.name: Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles

1-4.bio:
St. Apollinaria was the daughter of a Roman official of high rank in the fifth century. Tradition relates that she fled the world, disguised herself as a man, and lived as a monk in the Egyptian desert under the name Dorotheos, her identity being discovered only after her repose.

She is commemorated on January 4.
1-4.desc: Venerable Apollinaria, who lived in disguise as a monk in the Egyptian desert.
1-4.name: Apollinaria the Senator's Daughter

1-4.bio:
St. Nikephoros the Leper was born in Crete in 1890 and contracted leprosy as a youth. He became a monk and spent decades in the leper colony of Chios and later in Athens, blinded and crippled by his disease, yet radiant with patience, prayer, and joy.

He reposed in 1964 and was glorified as a saint in 2012. Many turn to him for help in illness. He is commemorated on January 4.
1-4.desc: Venerable Nikephoros the Leper, a Greek ascetic of the twentieth century who bore leprosy with thanksgiving.
1-4.name: Nikephoros the Leper

1-4.bio:
St. Euthymios was abbot of the Vatopedi Monastery on Mount Athos in the thirteenth century. When the Latinizing party under Michael VIII sought to impose the union with Rome on the Holy Mountain, he and twelve of his monks refused; tradition relates that he was drowned and the others hanged.

They are commemorated on January 4 as confessors of the Orthodox faith.
1-4.desc: Abbot Euthymios and twelve monks of Vatopedi, martyred for resisting the union with Rome.
1-4.name: Euthymios of Vatopedi and the Twelve Monks

1-4.bio:
St. Onouphrios was born in Bulgaria and became a monk at the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos. Having once as a child spoken words of denial in anger, he sought to atone by open confession, and with the blessing of his elders went to Chios, where he was beheaded for Christ in 1818.

He is commemorated on January 4.
1-4.desc: New Monk-Martyr Onouphrios of Hilandar, martyred on Chios in the nineteenth century.
1-4.name: Onouphrios the New of Hilandar

1-4.bio:
St. Theoktistos was abbot of a monastery at Cucomo in Sicily and reposed in peace in the ninth century. The synaxaria remember him for his ascetic life and the guidance he gave his brotherhood.

He is commemorated on January 4.
1-4.desc: Venerable Theoktistos, abbot of the monastery of Cucomo in Sicily.
1-4.name: Theoktistos of Cucomo

1-5.bio:
St. Theopemptos was a bishop who suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Tradition relates that his steadfastness under torture so moved a pagan sorcerer named Theonas that he too confessed Christ, was baptized, and shared in the crown of martyrdom.

Together the bishop and the converted sorcerer bear witness that the courage of the martyrs was itself a preaching of the Gospel. They are commemorated on January 5, the eve of Theophany.
1-5.name: Theopemptos

1-5.bio:
St. Synkletike was born to a wealthy family of Alexandria in the fourth century. After the death of her parents she gave away her inheritance and withdrew with her blind sister to a tomb outside the city, where a community of women gathered around her.

Her sayings on prayer, humility, and the spiritual struggle are preserved among those of the Desert Fathers. She bore a long illness in her old age with great patience and reposed in peace. She is commemorated on January 5.
1-5.desc: Venerable Synkletike, mother of women's monasticism in Egypt.
1-5.name: Synkletike of Alexandria

1-5.bio:
St. Theonas was a sorcerer who, tradition relates, was sent to poison the Hieromartyr Theopemptos of Nicomedia during the persecution of Diocletian. Seeing the bishop unharmed, he believed in Christ and was baptized.

He was martyred together with Theopemptos, and the two are commemorated on January 5.
1-5.desc: Holy Martyr Theonas, the magician converted by the Hieromartyr Theopemptos.
1-5.name: Theonas the Martyr

1-5.bio:
St. Romanos was born near Karpenisi and became a monk. Tradition relates that he longed for martyrdom, went to Constantinople, and there openly confessed Christ before the authorities; he was beheaded in 1694.

He is commemorated on January 5.
1-5.desc: New Monk-Martyr Romanos, martyred in Constantinople in the seventeenth century.
1-5.name: Romanos of Karpenisi

1-5.bio: St. Domnina is commemorated on January 5 as a venerable woman who lived in asceticism and reposed in peace. The synaxaria preserve little beyond the record of her holy life.
1-5.name: Domnina the Venerable

1-5.bio:
St. Phosterios was a hermit whose name means the light-bearing one. Tradition relates that he lived on a mountain in solitude, was fed by God's providence, and drew many to repentance by his example before reposing in peace.

He is commemorated on January 5.
1-5.desc: Venerable Phosterios, a hermit who shone in the ascetic life.
1-5.name: Phosterios the Hermit

1-5.bio:
St. Gregory of Akrita was born in Crete in the eighth century and became a monk. After pilgrimage to the Holy Land he settled at the monastery of Akrita near Constantinople, where he lived in strict asceticism through the iconoclast troubles.

He reposed in peace and is commemorated on January 5.
1-5.desc: Venerable Gregory of Akrita, a monk of Crete and Constantinople.
1-5.name: Gregory of Akrita

1-6.bio:
The Feast of Theophany, or Epiphany, commemorates the Baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ by St. John the Forerunner in the River Jordan. As Christ came up from the waters, the heavens opened, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father was heard — the first clear revelation of the Holy Trinity.
