One of the twelve Great Feasts, Theophany celebrates the sanctification of the waters and of all creation. On this day the Church performs the Great Blessing of the Waters, and in Greek tradition the cross is cast into the sea and retrieved by swimmers as a blessing for the new year.
1-6.desc: The Epiphany — Baptism of the Lord Jesus Christ in the Jordan.
1-6.name: Theophany

1-6.bio:
St. Romanos was born in the region of Sparta in the Peloponnese. Tradition relates that he was captured by the Turks, refused to renounce Christ, and after suffering was beheaded in Constantinople in 1695.

He is commemorated on January 6, the day of the Theophany.
1-6.desc: New Martyr Romanos of Sparta, martyred in Constantinople in the seventeenth century.
1-6.name: Romanos the Lacedaemonian

1-6.bio:
St. Theophan the Recluse was a Russian bishop of the nineteenth century who, after serving as Bishop of Tambov and Vladimir, retired to the Vysha Monastery and lived in seclusion for over twenty years. From his cell he wrote extensively on the spiritual life and carried on a vast correspondence of counsel.

He translated the Philokalia into Russian and reposed in 1894 on the feast of the Theophany. He is commemorated on January 6.
1-6.desc: St. Theophan the Recluse, Bishop of Tambov, spiritual writer.
1-6.name: Theophan the Recluse

1-7.bio:
On the day after Theophany, the Church gathers to honor St. John the Forerunner and Baptist, the greatest of the prophets, who was found worthy to baptize the Lord in the Jordan. Son of the priest Zacharias and the righteous Elizabeth, John lived in the wilderness in fasting and prayer, preaching repentance and preparing the way of the Lord.

Christ Himself said that among those born of women none had arisen greater than John. He completed his witness as a martyr, beheaded by Herod for rebuking his unlawful marriage. This Synaxis on January 7 is one of the most celebrated name days in the Greek world.
1-7.desc: Feast of the Holy Forerunner and Baptist John.
1-7.name: John the Baptist

1-7.bio:
St. Athanasios was born in Attaleia in Asia Minor and lived in Smyrna. Tradition relates that after being accused of having spoken words of conversion to Islam, he refused to abandon the Christian faith and was beheaded in Smyrna in 1700.

He is commemorated on January 7.
1-7.desc: New Martyr Athanasios of Attaleia, martyred in Smyrna.
1-7.name: Athanasios of Attaleia

1-7.bio:
St. Julian was a deacon from the island of Aegina, remembered in the synaxaria as a martyr for Christ. Few details of his contest have been preserved.

He is commemorated on January 7.
1-7.desc: Holy Martyr Julian the Deacon, of Aegina.
1-7.name: Julian the Deacon of Aegina

1-7.bio:
St. Cedd was a monk of Lindisfarne in the seventh century, one of four brothers who became priests. He preached the Gospel among the Middle Angles and the East Saxons, was consecrated bishop, and founded the monastery of Lastingham in Yorkshire.

He reposed of the plague in 664 and is commemorated on January 7.
1-7.desc: St. Cedd, missionary bishop of the East Saxons.
1-7.name: Cedd of Lastingham

1-8.bio:
St. George the Chozebite was born on the island of Cyprus and became a monk of the monastery of Choziba, in the wild gorge on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho. Living in the seventh century, he embraced great austerity, humility, and unceasing prayer, and in time guided the brotherhood as a spiritual father.

His life, recorded by his disciple, preserves the memory of a gentle and severe ascetic in the tradition of the desert fathers of Palestine. He is commemorated on January 8.
1-8.name: George the Chozebite

1-8.bio:
St. Domnika came from Carthage to Constantinople in the late fourth century, where she was baptized by the Patriarch Nektarios. She founded a convent in the city and became famous for her ascetic life and gift of prophecy.

She reposed in peace at a great age and is commemorated on January 8.
1-8.name: Domnika of Constantinople

1-8.bio:
St. Kyranna was a young woman from the village of Avysoka near Thessaloniki. In 1751, having refused the advances of a Turkish officer and the demand that she change her faith, she was imprisoned and beaten to death.

Tradition relates that a heavenly light shone in her cell at the moment of her death. She is commemorated on January 8.
1-8.desc: Virgin New Martyr Kyranna of Thessaloniki.
1-8.name: Kyranna the New Martyr

1-8.bio:
St. Carterios was a priest of Caesarea in Cappadocia who instructed many in the faith and built a church for his flock. In the persecution under Diocletian he was arrested, tortured, and finally pierced with a spear.

He is commemorated on January 8.
1-8.desc: Hieromartyr Carterios, priest and teacher of Caesarea in Cappadocia.
1-8.name: Carterios of Caesarea

1-8.bio:
Sts. Julian and Basilissa were a married couple of Antinoe in Egypt who lived in virginity by mutual agreement and turned their houses into monasteries. In the persecution under Diocletian, Julian was arrested after Basilissa's peaceful repose and suffered martyrdom with many others, among them the priest Antony and the boy Celsus.

They are commemorated on January 8.
1-8.desc: Holy Martyrs Julian and Basilissa of Egypt and those with them.
1-8.name: Julian and Basilissa

1-8.bio: St. Agathon is commemorated on January 8 as a venerable ascetic who reposed in peace. Tradition remembers him for his humility and gentleness in the monastic life.
1-8.name: Agathon the Venerable

1-8.bio:
St. Abo was an Arab perfumer from Baghdad who came to Georgia in the eighth century and, drawn by the faith of the people, was baptized. He preached Christ openly in Tbilisi under Muslim rule and was beheaded in 786.

He is honored as a patron of Tbilisi and is commemorated on January 8.
1-8.desc: Holy Martyr Abo the Perfumer, patron of Tbilisi.
1-8.name: Abo of Tbilisi

1-9.bio:
St. Polyeuktos was a Roman soldier in Melitene of Armenia in the third century, and is honored as the first martyr of that city. Moved by the faith of his Christian friend Nearchos, he confessed Christ openly, refused to honor the idols, and was beheaded for the Lord he had only newly come to know.

His martyrdom sealed a friendship in Christ that the Church has remembered ever since, and a famous church in Constantinople later bore his name. He is commemorated on January 9.
1-9.name: Polyeuktos

1-9.bio:
St. Eustratios was born in Bithynia and became a monk at the Augaros Monastery on Mount Olympus in the ninth century. He suffered exile during the iconoclast persecution and later governed his monastery for many years, receiving the gift of miracles.

He reposed in peace at a great age and is commemorated on January 9.
1-9.desc: Venerable Eustratios, abbot of the Augaros Monastery in Bithynia.
1-9.name: Eustratios the Wonderworker

1-9.bio:
St. Peter was the youngest brother of St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nyssa, raised by their sister St. Makrina. He became abbot of the monastery founded by Basil on the river Iris and later Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia.

He took part in the Second Ecumenical Council and reposed in peace. He is commemorated on January 9.
1-9.desc: St. Peter, Bishop of Sebaste, brother of St. Basil the Great.
1-9.name: Peter of Sebaste

1-9.bio:
St. Antonina was a Christian woman of Nicomedia who confessed Christ during the persecutions. Tradition relates that after torture she was sewn into a sack and cast into the sea.

She is commemorated on January 9.
1-9.desc: Holy Martyr Antonina, who suffered at Nicomedia.
1-9.name: Antonina of Nicomedia

1-9.bio:
St. Philip was abbot of the Solovki Monastery and became Metropolitan of Moscow in 1566. He openly denounced the cruelty of Tsar Ivan the Terrible and his oprichniki, refusing him a blessing in the cathedral, and for this was deposed and imprisoned.

He was strangled in his monastic prison in 1569. He is commemorated on January 9.
1-9.desc: Hieromartyr Philip, Metropolitan of Moscow, who rebuked Ivan the Terrible.
1-9.name: Philip of Moscow
